Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

WHEN THE INTERNET IS SHUT DOWN, THE RIGHT TO COMMUNICATE DOESN’T SIMPLY DISAPPEAR

The BitChat episode raises a much bigger question than one app.

BitChat is designed to allow nearby phones to communicate through Bluetooth mesh, without depending on mobile internet, SIM cards or a central messaging server. Its popularity reportedly surged in India during protests where internet connectivity was restricted.

On 3 October 2026, Apple removed BitChat from the Indian App Store following a government direction under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act. The Internet Freedom Foundation has questioned the legality and proportionality of blocking an entire communications application, particularly when the specific allegedly unlawful content has not been publicly identified.

The democratic principle is simple:

Internet shutdown ≠ shutdown of citizenship.

A democracy must be able to distinguish between:
• unlawful conduct and lawful communication;
• specific harmful content and an entire communications tool;
• legitimate security concerns and disproportionate restrictions;
• regulation and suppression of the ability of citizens to communicate.

The answer to concerns about misuse should be due process, transparency and targeted action—not automatically making ordinary citizens unable to communicate with one another.

The government should publicly disclose the legal basis and specific grounds for the blocking order, and affected developers should have meaningful access to legal remedies.

Technology will keep evolving. Democratic safeguards must evolve with it.

Protect communication. Protect due process. Protect the constitutional space for peaceful citizenship.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

High speed internet for everyone is welcome. 🙏🏻

But before Starlink is treated as a public good in India, a few questions need clear answers.

If the US government requests Indian user metadata, traffic patterns, or location data, will Starlink comply? Under what law, and with what notice to India?

Would Starlink assist a US operation targeting an Indian official or asset the way commercial platforms have cooperated in other US actions abroad?

What is the license term, and what happens to ground stations, spectrum, and customer data if India later runs its own LEO constellation?

Is foreign entry being slowed because ISRO and Indian operators are already building domestic satcom capacity, or only because incumbents want to protect market share?

Where is Indian user data stored and processed? Can it be compelled from US soil under the CLOUD Act or a national-security letter?

Who controls shutdown, geofencing, and service denial in a border or internal-security crisis — Starlink, the US government, or Indian authorities?

What local ownership, security audit, and lawful-intercept commitments match what India already requires of other telecom operators?

Answer those in public, then the oligarch claim can be tested against the record. 🙏🏻

Mobile Internet Shut Off Near Connaught Place, IFF Flags Lack of Suspension Order

'The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when,' the internet freedom watchdog said in a statement.

Keep Starlink out.

Imagine paying your internet bill on time, only to discover your connection also needs good relations with Washington. India’s connectivity should never depend on another country’s approval.

For example, when Visa and Mastercard suspended operations in Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, Russian-issued cards stopped working abroad. Domestic payments survived because Russia had its own infrastructure.

That’s the concern with Starlink: foreign control over connectivity, questions about data privacy, and dependence that becomes expensive to undo. While the company claims to be independent, what happens when Washington demands otherwise?

India should keep it out unless those risks are addressed. “Terms and conditions apply” is fine for a discount coupon. Less reassuring for national sovereignty.

text: @elonmusk Yes, India needs Starlink. But what assurance can you give that Starlink won't be misused for anti-national activities during an internet shutdown?

WHEN THE INTERNET IS SHUT DOWN, THE RIGHT TO COMMUNICATE DOESN’T SIMPLY DISAPPEAR

The BitChat episode raises a much bigger question than one app.

BitChat is designed to allow nearby phones to communicate through Bluetooth mesh, without depending on mobile internet, SIM cards or a central messaging server. Its popularity reportedly surged in India during protests where internet connectivity was restricted.

On 3 October 2026, Apple removed BitChat from the Indian App Store following a government direction under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act. The Internet Freedom Foundation has questioned the legality and proportionality of blocking an entire communications application, particularly when the specific allegedly unlawful content has not been publicly identified.

The democratic principle is simple:

Internet shutdown ≠ shutdown of citizenship.

A democracy must be able to distinguish between:
• unlawful conduct and lawful communication;
• specific harmful content and an entire communications tool;
• legitimate security concerns and disproportionate restrictions;
• regulation and suppression of the ability of citizens to communicate.

The answer to concerns about misuse should be due process, transparency and targeted action—not automatically making ordinary citizens unable to communicate with one another.

The government should publicly disclose the legal basis and specific grounds for the blocking order, and affected developers should have meaningful access to legal remedies.

Technology will keep evolving. Democratic safeguards must evolve with it.

Protect communication. Protect due process. Protect the constitutional space for peaceful citizenship.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

🚨India’s Crackdown on Illegal Immigration Enters a Jammu Kashmir: IAF Jets Move 300 Bangladeshis From J&K to West Bengal Border, Are Rohingyas Next?

Around 600 Bangladeshi nationals have reportedly been identified in the Kashmir Valley. The first 150 were flown from Srinagar to Bagdogra in an Indian Air Force aircraft, where they were handed over to the BSF for onward repatriation. Another 150 are being moved, taking the first phase to 300 people.

The operation follows document checks, police verification and confirmation of nationality through official channels. From Bagdogra, the deportees are expected to be taken towards the India-Bangladesh border and formally handed over to Bangladeshi authorities.

But the bigger question is now emerging: Are the Rohingyas next?

Thousands of Rohingyas have been identified in Jammu & Kashmir, and authorities have already acted against alleged unauthorised settlements and encroachments. However, their deportation is far more complicated. Bangladesh already hosts a massive Rohingya population, while repatriation to Myanmar faces serious verification, acceptance and security challenges.

The J&K crackdown therefore represents more than a deportation drive. It highlights a broader policy challenge for India: identifying illegal foreign nationals, establishing their nationality, removing unauthorised settlements and, most importantly, creating a legally workable mechanism to return those who are found to be unlawfully residing in the country.

The Bangladesh cases may be the beginning. The much harder question is what comes next for the Rohingyas.

70 naali of illegal bhang destroyed in Chamoli. But what if hemp could be part of the answer?

Under the “Drugs Free Devbhoomi” campaign, Chamoli Police destroyed illegal cannabis being grown on around 70 naali of land in Rampur Tok, Dewal. The joint team included the SOG, Dewal police outpost, Social Welfare Department, Legal Services Authority and Forest Department.

The team told villagers about the legal consequences of illegal cannabis cultivation and the harms of drug abuse, and asked them to destroy wild cannabis growing nearby too. SOG in-charge SI Satendra Butola also warned villagers about cyber fraud, including fake KYC, online investment scams, digital arrest and suspicious links, and urged them to report it on 1930.

Stopping drug abuse matters. But this story also raises a bigger question.
For years, we’ve talked about how to create jobs and income in the hills. Meanwhile, monkeys and wild boars have ruined so many fields that families have simply stopped farming, and terraces lie empty. Farmers in the hills often say cannabis is one crop wild animals leave alone.

Industrial hemp, the low-THC variety that can’t be used as a drug, is used for fibre, textiles, rope, seed oil, building material and medicines. Uttarakhand was actually the first state in India to legalise industrial hemp cultivation. But years later, it has struggled to build proper markets and workable rules, so it never really took off.

Now Himachal Pradesh is trying to do it properly, replacing wild cannabis with state-licensed industrial hemp under a 0.3% THC limit. It expects the sector to bring in $120 to $240 million a year once it scales up.

Uttarakhand had the idea first. Instead of only destroying crops every season, what if the state made legal hemp a real option, with licences, seeds, buyers and support? It could bring income back to the hills and give people a reason to stay.

The End of Ordinary Politics 

'When order is reconstituted, the instruments of the previous regime are taken over rather than replaced. As it happened at the founding of the Republic, its transition to a Hindutva order was quickly followed by a reframing of what is legitimate politics. The long journey of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act over many decades through various regimes is instructive. Since 2019, individuals, and not only organisations, can be notified as ‘terrorist’. Mere association with an illegal outfit makes an individual liable regardless of the commission of any illegal act. The Supreme Court of India told protestors at Shaheen Bagh (2019-20) that they must act within the bounds of law. Any criticism of the government is portrayed as anti-national; restrictions on freedom of expression are enforced for undisclosed national security reasons, and foreign links make any opinion questionable. Simultaneously, the Ayodhya insurrection has been legitimised as a sovereign act through a judicial process, retrospectively.

Much like those in power use the law and institutions, those who challenge them also can use it, but only to a limited extent. text:
Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

🚨UPDATE: the court has now delivered its orders.

The High Court has quashed the notices the Judicial Service Commission sent to the Supreme Court judges requiring them to answer the complaints. It gave three reasons.

✅ First, the Commission acted without a preliminary assessment. It took up the complaints before carrying out the initial filtering the court said was required.

✅ Second, the complaints were omnibus. They swept many grievances, and several judges, into single blanket removal complaints, instead of putting a specific and detailed case to each judge.

✅ Third, the complaints attacked the merits of judgments. Where a party is unhappy with a decision, the proper path is review or appeal, not a petition to remove the judge who made it. The removal process cannot stand in for an appeal.

The through line is simple. The right to complain about a judge is real, but it has limits, and here those limits were crossed.

quotedTweet.text:
🚨 Happening now. The High Court is delivering judgment in a landmark standoff between the judges of the Supreme Court of Kenya and the body that can recommend their removal from office.

The background. Every judge of the Supreme Court went to the High Court to challenge whether the Judicial Service Commission, the body that handles complaints against judges, can entertain complaints that are really an attack on the merits of their judgments. In plain terms, the judges say a party who loses a case should not be able to turn the complaints process into a second appeal against a decision they did not like.

The matter is before a three judge bench of Justices Kariuki, Mugambi and Mwamuye.
A caveat first. The judgment is still being read from the bench as we write. What follows is the court's reasoning so far, and it is not final until the court concludes.
The determination so far. The decision appears to be unanimous, and the court framed seven issues for determination. 
Three already stand out.

✅ First, on the court's own power to hear the case. Under Article 165 of the Constitution, the High Court holds supervisory jurisdiction. The independence given to the Commission is not the same as immunity. Its actions, and its failures to act, can be examined in court, because no public body sits above the Constitution, and the court may inquire whether what the Commission did was constitutional.

✅ Second, on what the Commission must do before calling a judge to answer. The court held that the Commission is not a mere postbox that receives a complaint and forwards it on. It must carry out an initial threshold assessment and filter out complaints that are frivolous.

✅ Third, on running two processes at once. Where a complainant takes the same grievance to the High Court and to the Commission at the same time, there is no blanket rule, but the court must look at the real substance of both. Where they genuinely overlap, pursuing both can amount to an abuse of the court process.

On one side is the independence of the Judiciary. A judge must be free to decide a case without fear that the losing party will retaliate with a removal complaint. On the other is accountability. The Commission has a constitutional duty to receive genuine complaints about how judges conduct themselves, and that duty should not be hollowed out. The hard line is between a true complaint about how a judge behaved and a disguised appeal against what a judge decided.

✅ Four further issues remain to be read, and the final orders will show how far the court has gone.

👉 Follow @Lexken_EMSLaw for practical legal insights on constitutional law and the Judiciary.

A man was arrested in Rajasthan after investigators say he used AI-generated videos of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and actor Vijay to lure people into a financial scam.

The fake videos showed Vijay speaking Hindi and were distributed through Facebook and other social platforms. Targets were then moved into WhatsApp conversations connected to the alleged fraud.

There's a useful pattern here.

The deepfake doesn't necessarily have to complete the scam.

It has to establish enough trust to get you to the next step.

That's how modern fraud funnels work.

Attention

You see a recognizable person in your feed.

Trust

They're apparently recommending an investment.

Migration

You're directed to WhatsApp, Telegram, a website or another private channel.

Conversion

Someone asks for money, credentials or personal information.

People tend to focus on the first step:

Could I recognize that the video was fake?

That's becoming the least reliable defense.

The better defense is to examine the transaction.

A celebrity recommends an investment?

Don't click the link in the post.

Search independently.

Go to the person's verified website or known account.

Check whether the investment appears there.

Then investigate the company.

Who owns it?

How long has the domain existed?

Is the business registered?

Does the regulator recognize it?

Where is your money actually being sent?

The face in the video is becoming decoration.

AI can reproduce it.

The transaction leaves harder evidence.

A bank account has an owner.

A domain has history.

A company has records.

A wallet has transactions.

A phone number has patterns.

A website has infrastructure.

That's where verification should move.

The deepfake era is teaching us something uncomfortable:

Recognition is no longer authentication.

"I know that face" used to carry information.

Increasingly, it doesn't.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

What exactly are we achieving?

If one Telugu film loses, Telugu cinema does not win.

The cake is big enough for everyone to have a piece.

As President of the Movie Artistes Association, I want to make it clear that MAA is compiling information on accounts and networks repeatedly involved in targeted abuse and malicious campaigns, including accounts misusing actors’ photographs and identities to mislead people.

This is NOT about stopping criticism.

It is about accountability.

The present deepfake incident makes the larger conversation urgent. And unfortunately, this will not be the last deepfake. Technology is moving too quickly for us to believe deleting one video or filing one complaint solves the problem.

I request the Telugu Film Chamber, Producers Council, MAA and all stakeholders to sit together and create a permanent industry-wide mechanism to address AI deepfakes, impersonation, coordinated malicious campaigns and deliberate online sabotage.

Not another meeting that ends with a photograph.

Not another phone call.

A SYSTEM.

We may compete every Friday.

But we cannot spend the rest of the week trying to destroy one another.

Let audiences decide the fate of our films.

Let cinema win 🙏

A false no-show is one tool. These are the others that show up in the record, in OIG audits, and in claim files. Some are policy. Some are bad data that the agency then treats as fact. The effect on the veteran is the same.
The chart is written against him. “Veteran refused,” “noncompliant,” “no acute distress,” and “ambulating without difficulty” get entered when he was in pain, unstable, or never examined the way the note says. A later rater, nurse, or judge reads that note as the truth. Amendment requests go to the same facility. Privacy officers deny them. The false note stays, and every new decision cites it.
Scheduling numbers are protected, not the veteran. OIG has repeatedly found clinic cancellations entered as “canceled by patient,” hidden wait lists, and off-books tracking. The computer shows a short wait. The veteran waits months. A no-show or a patient-cancel code keeps the miss off the facility’s access report.
Consults die on a timer. Miss the appointment, miss the callback, or miss a letter, and staff can discontinue the consult without a doctor reviewing it. Community-care consults are worse. In the first quarter of fiscal 2025, OIG found about 45 percent of VA consults and 60 percent of community-care consults missed the scheduling standard, and about half of both missed the standard for actually being seen. Eligible veterans are also scheduled inside VA with no record they were told they could go outside. The MISSION Act right exists on paper and not in the scheduler’s screen.
Outside records never make it back. OIG found that of nearly 3 million closed community-care consults in one review window, a large share were closed without the outside notes in the VA chart, and tens of thousands sat open more than 90 days past the appointment. The veteran was treated. The VA file says he was not, or says nothing. The next clinician treats the gap as no history.
The claim exam is built to deny. VA must order a C&P exam when the file shows a current disability, an in-service event, and any indication of a link. It often does not. When it does, examiners check “less likely than not” with no rationale, ignore lay statements, and do not review the file. Under Barr v. Nicholson that exam is legally inadequate. VA denies on it anyway. The appeal finds the duty-to-assist error years later and sends it back for another exam by the same system.
A missed C&P is treated as abandonment. Miss the exam without what VA calls good cause and the claim can be denied for failure to report. The veteran’s own medical records do not fill the hole. Rescheduling is a favor, not a right, once they have marked him absent.
Private evidence is discounted on sight. A treating doctor’s nexus or DBQ is called less probative than a VA examiner who saw him once. The file then says the favorable opinion was “not adequate,” and the denial rests on the VA opinion alone.

Users can choose to open the retailer's website after clicking a list, or open it inside the Muse app and check out with the agent.
⠀
When they choose agent checkout, Muse prepares the checkout flow in advance, shows an 'approval card' with order details for the user to confirm, and requires the user to give access to email, full name, and address.
⠀
Payment can go through Link by Stripe, Meta's payment partner, or Shopify ($SHOP) Shop Pay; the user has to link Shop Pay; Link creates one-time cards to hide the real card number.
⠀
Meta says PayPal ($PYPL) has been announced as a payment provider for Muse, but it is not live yet.

▋ The fast lane arrives but not all connectors are live
⠀
Meta announced on September 23 that it built a group of retail partners for the Muse platform, including Walmart ($WMT), Gap ($GAP), Sephora, Expedia ($EXPE), Wayfair ($W), Best Buy ($BBY), and others, and called it the 'official fast lane' for the Muse agent platform.
⠀
CNBC noted that not all of what it called 'connectors' are live.
⠀
Ticketmaster, which was included in the partner list, said final purchases still happen inside its own secure marketplace.
⠀
CNBC quoted its spokesperson as saying consumers keep full control over purchase decisions.
⠀
Crypto Briefing reported that Muse runs on the Muse Spark 1.3 model, has a 1 million token context window, and operates in a sandbox environment Meta calls Muse Secure VM to protect user data and financial information.
⠀
Zuckerberg previously teased a future model codenamed 'Watermelon' that The Information reported Meta planned for October, but as of October 6 it has not been officially released nor confirmed as Spark 1.3's direct successor.
⠀
Muse has a free plan, and paid plans are Power at $20 per month and Maximum at $100 per month.

▋ Amazon keeps its block up after the credential dispute
⠀
Amazon ($AMZN) started blocking Meta's Muse from completing purchases on Amazon on the evening of September 20, 2026.
⠀
It deployed an anti-bot wall, so Muse users on iOS, Android, and WhatsApp were cut off when they tried to reach Amazon, and a popup appeared saying they violated Amazon's terms of use.
⠀
CNBC reported that Amazon blocked Muse from buying products on Amazon's website because of a terms of service violation, and Amazon said Muse stores customer credentials and scrapes account data.
⠀
The e-commerce giant stated that Meta never notified it or got authorization before Muse accessed https://t.co/d2eVnDxN9g and operated inside customer accounts.
⠀
More critically, it pointed out that Muse did not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing; Amazon alleged Muse retrieves and stores customer credentials, raising privacy concerns.
⠀
Meta clarified that user login credentials are kept in isolated secure storage, and the Muse model itself cannot see passwords or payment methods.
⠀
Despite the clarification, the block remains in place.
⠀
A company spokesperson said third-party apps that buy for customers should work openly and respect whether a service provider wants to take part.
⠀
GeekWire reported that Amazon asked Meta to remove Amazon from that experience.
⠀
Both companies are currently in direct talks about the matter.
⠀
When asked whether it is considering legal action, the company declined to comment.

▋ Zuckerberg wants a sales cut but keeps the rate quiet
⠀
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said at Meta Connect that the company will charge a small fee on Muse transactions.
⠀
Yahoo Finance reporter Daniel Howley reported Zuckerberg told developers at Meta Connect 'We believe that Muse will make you money', and said Meta is backing that up first by offering lots of free tokens, with long-term profit expected to come from small fees on transactions.
⠀
On The Verge 'Sources' podcast, Zuckerberg told Alex Heath that Meta will 'take a very small cut of whatever the transaction is', with the cost borne by merchants that transact with users.
⠀
Ainvest's analysis said Zuckerberg did not provide a cut number, 'very small' is not a specific number, and Muse had no transaction volume, no reported revenue item, and was only available in the U.S. at the time.
⠀
The analysis noted users themselves do not pay; the cost is borne by businesses on the other side of the transaction.
⠀
Analysts note transaction fees are expected to be one of Muse's long-term monetization paths, but there is no indication Meta will abandon subscriptions, as it explores subscriptions, transaction fees, and enterprise services together.
⠀
Zuckerberg said at Meta Connect that Meta expects to profit by charging small fees on transactions that agents complete for users, and will first offer lots of free tokens to attract users.
⠀
In fact, Meta's second-quarter revenue was $60.8 billion, with $59.4 billion from advertising, while Muse currently has no ads at all.
⠀
Yahoo Finance, citing Benzinga, reported Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick said on CNBC's 'Mad Money' with host Jim Cramer that Meta is evaluating multiple ways to monetize Muse, including transaction fees and paid subscriptions.
⠀
She explained on the show: 'Muse is saving a lot of people money right now, so we are thinking about, as Mark said last week, the possibility of charging when we save you money.'
⠀
During the interview, she also launched Muse for small businesses to help owners manage cash flow, inventory, website design, and customer communications.
⠀
Behind that push is Meta's 3.6 billion Family daily active people (DAP) and 200 million small businesses, with lab AI products aimed at making the core business stronger.
⠀
Addressing security concerns, McCormick noted Meta delayed Muse's launch by 30 days to make sure the product was safe, encrypted, and error-free before launch.
⠀
In addition, Meta opened the connector platform and continues to expand its Meta Business Agent—launched back in June—which helps businesses answer questions, recommend products, book appointments, and qualify leads.
⠀
The article said the biggest signal is the Shopify partnership, which lets Muse browse merchant catalogs and complete purchases with Shop Pay.
⠀
On their own, these features do not bring in much revenue, but they add supply of goods and services for the agent to take a cut from.

▋ Behind outside agent blocks, Amazon guards ad revenue and direct relationships
⠀
GeekWire reported Amazon has huge business interests: beyond its flagship e-commerce site, Amazon generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, and that business depends on people browsing its pages and seeing sponsored products.
⠀
Over the past year, Amazon has tried to keep outside agents away from its website, including suing Perplexity over the Comet browser and moving to block shopping agents from Google ($GOOGL) and OpenAI.
⠀
Amazon's own agentic shopping feature Buy for Me identifies itself and lets brands opt out.
⠀
In a related legal clash, the company won a preliminary injunction against Perplexity in March, but the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned it on August 4, ruling that users rather than the AI company accessed computers under federal anti-hacking laws.
⠀
While a rehearing request was denied on September 10, the ruling still leaves Amazon a path to pursue claims based on contract and terms of service.
⠀
An AI Business Review analysis pointed out the block weakens Muse's core value proposition, because shopping is the key use case for AI agents.
⠀
With eMarketer estimating Amazon accounted for about 38% of U.S. ecommerce sales in 2023, its catalog is difficult to replace.
⠀
The retail landscape has begun to divide: Walmart, Gap, Best Buy, and Shopify have embraced agentic shopping, while Amazon, Kohl's, and eBay impose restrictions, and brands like Tapestry allow browsing but limit direct transactions.
⠀
Overseas, while Amazon Marketplace is subject to the EU Digital Markets Act, current DMA rules do not explicitly mandate accepting unauthorized shopping agents, though differential treatment could trigger competition scrutiny.
⠀
The analysis noted regulatory attention could soon follow.

▋ Shopping inside the agent puts brand traffic at risk
⠀
Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business who studies psychological responses to AI, told CNBC that pushing shopping into a single agentic shopping experience will intensify competition among shopping giants.
⠀
He said 'the real battlefield for Muse is among companies, and consumers are the prize', and 'whoever owns the agent owns the relationship with the shopper'.
⠀
CNN cited IDC analyst Francisco Jeronimo saying Meta has done a better job than other tech giants at showing consumers what Muse can do.
⠀
'Others have not promoted agent shopping as hard as Meta has through Muse, and I think that is the main difference,' he explained.
⠀
The network also quoted Kathryn Heinz, Expedia vice president of enterprise alliances and AI, saying Expedia chose to allow AI agents because it wants to 'show up wherever travelers search', and added that about two-thirds of Expedia's traffic comes from its own platforms.
⠀
Market reaction was swift: following the announcement, travel stocks faced re-evaluation, with shares of Expedia, Airbnb, and Booking experiencing temporary dips between 5% and 7%.
⠀
Yet agentic shopping brings broader friction: if purchases stay inside assistant apps, brand website traffic could drop alongside direct customer engagement.
⠀
Brands could also lose the ability to understand customer shopping habits or drive add-on purchases through in-app promotions and recommendations.
⠀
A Yahoo Tech analysis emphasized responsibility is a problem at the center of this dispute: if Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers bear the returns and disputes, rather than Meta.
⠀
Online restaurant reservation platform Resy also stated it 'currently does not allow unapproved third-party bots or agents' to access its service.
⠀
The platform temporarily locked a user's account after another assistant, Instinct, sent around 200 API requests per hour to monitor open tables.

▋ Dynamic pricing fears grow while Meta's platform governance faces scrutiny
⠀
CNBC cited a January survey from Morning Consult that found 59% of U.S. adults said price gouging is a 'major concern' when it comes to AI-driven dynamic pricing.
⠀
Seeking to reassure shoppers, Walmart CEO John Furner published an open letter promising not to use shoppers' personal information to run dynamic pricing on its website or shopping tools.
⠀
Still, Meta's broader record on privacy, child safety, and platform governance presents a high trust bar, following a court-approved multistate settlement of nearly $17 billion.

▋ Early downloads spike but the real test starts when free tokens run out
⠀
Crypto Briefing and Reuters reported the Muse app reached roughly 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks, and surpassed 5 million cumulative downloads by late September.
⠀
Yahoo Finance cited Sensor Tower estimating DAU at roughly 560,000 on the app's eleventh day, while Ainvest noted the app hit the top of the Apple App Store within a week.
⠀
Cantor Fitzgerald analysts described Muse's early unit economics as 'subsidized'.
⠀
Download surges are typical for heavily promoted launches; the true retention test begins once free tokens run dry.
⠀
Meanwhile, Meta projects full-year 2026 total capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion, with AI infrastructure as a primary driver.
⠀
On a trailing twelve months (TTM) basis, capital expenditures ran near $92 billion against $38.5 billion in free cash flow, which dropped 23%.
⠀
Analysts interpret that heavy spending as aggressive investment rather than structural deterioration.
⠀
Wall Street remains largely optimistic on early traction, with Wells Fargo ($WFC) and KeyBanc Capital Markets raising Meta price targets.

▋ Hardware aims for the holidays while more retail partners join
⠀
Looking ahead to hardware, Zuckerberg announced Muse will arrive on Meta's AI glasses, along with an upcoming pocket device called Muse Charm, noting the team's goal is to launch it before the holidays.
⠀
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang confirmed Meta added PayPal support and announced integrations with retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Wayfair, and American Eagle ($AEO).
⠀
For travel, it added Expedia integration, and for grocery shopping, it brought Instacart ($CART) into Muse.
⠀
A Meta spokesperson told CNBC that shopping has quickly become one of the biggest reasons people use Muse.
⠀
Amazon's block is still in place, Muse's shopping features are just getting started, and where consumers complete their next transaction depends on how wide these doors open.
